title: International Organizations II — the UN, and exam cases

slides.title: Admission to the UN: the conditions
slides.text: Article 4(1) sets four conditions and they are cumulative: the applicant must be a STATE, must be PEACE-LOVING, must ACCEPT the obligations of the Charter, and must — in the judgment of the Organization — be ABLE AND WILLING to carry them out. The last clause is what gives the political organs room to refuse; the ICJ has held that members may not add conditions beyond these, but the assessment of them is theirs.

cards.q: What are the conditions for admission to the United Nations under Article 4(1)?
cards.a: The applicant must be a state, peace-loving, must accept the Charter obligations, and must — in the judgment of the Organization — be able and willing to carry them out.

slides.title: Admission: the procedure
slides.text: Article 4(2) splits the decision between the two political organs: admission is effected by a decision of the General Assembly UPON THE RECOMMENDATION of the Security Council. Two consequences worth seeing. The Assembly cannot admit without a recommendation, so each permanent member's veto reaches admission; and the recommendation is a substantive, not a procedural, matter.

cards.q: Who decides on admission to the UN, and why can a single permanent member block it?
cards.a: The General Assembly decides upon the recommendation of the Security Council (Art 4(2)). Because the recommendation is a non-procedural decision, it is subject to the veto of any permanent member.

slides.title: Leaving, and being thrown out
slides.text: Withdrawal is sometimes expressly provided for — the EU is the example — and is regarded as permissible even without an express clause, because of sovereignty; Indonesia's brief withdrawal from the UN in 1965 is the precedent. Expulsion may be provided for where a member persistently violates its obligations, as in Article 6 of the Charter, but in practice organizations reach for softer tools: refusing to accept credentials, or suspending voting rights for non-payment of contributions under Article 19.

terms.def: Expulsion of a member which has persistently violated the Principles of the Charter, by the General Assembly upon the Security Council's recommendation.
Loss of vote in the General Assembly for a member in arrears by two years' contributions.

cards.q: May a state withdraw from an international organization whose founding treaty is silent on withdrawal?
cards.a: Yes, on the prevailing view, because of sovereignty — Indonesia's withdrawal from the UN in 1965 is the precedent. Express withdrawal clauses (as in the EU) only regulate the procedure.

cards.q: Which measures short of expulsion can an organization use against a recalcitrant member?
cards.a: Refusing to recognise its credentials, and suspending voting rights — in the UN, loss of the vote in the General Assembly for arrears of two years' contributions under Article 19.

slides.title: Who pays
slides.text: Three income streams. Assessed membership contributions, divided among members as percentages — the poorest states pay 0.001 per cent, the United States 22 per cent, China 20 per cent, Austria about 1 per cent, against a UN regular budget of $3.7 billion. Payment is a LEGAL OBLIGATION, and non-payment triggers sanctions such as loss of voting rights, which makes the scale of contributions effective leverage. Then voluntary contributions, which fund programmes, aid funds and peacekeeping — $5.6 billion in 2025. And independent income, such as the World Bank's lending.

cards.q: Why is the scale of assessed contributions politically significant, not merely financial?
cards.a: Because payment is a legal obligation whose breach carries sanctions such as loss of voting rights, a large contributor's threat to withhold payment is effective leverage over the organization.

slides.title: When a decision of an organ binds
slides.text: Two things decide: the tasks and competences of the organization or organ, and the INTENTION of the organ — the Security Council can issue both binding and non-binding decisions, so the same body's output must be read case by case. Behind this sits the standing tension between effective cooperation and preserving national freedom of action: a supranational organization like the EU takes binding decisions as a matter of course, and technical organizations bind more often than political ones.

cards.q: How do you determine whether a decision of an organ of an international organization is binding?
cards.a: By the competences of the organization and organ, and by the intention of the organ in that decision. The Security Council, for instance, issues both binding and non-binding acts — the wording and the legal basis reveal which.

slides.title: Recommendations are not nothing
slides.text: The diagram contrasts the two columns and the left one is the more interesting. Non-binding recommendations vary in authority but have legal effects nonetheless: a member must consider a recommendation in GOOD FAITH, and conduct that conforms to it benefits from a presumption of legality. They can also be catalysts — for custom, by evidencing opinio iuris, and for treaties — and they support arguments before courts. Binding decisions, by contrast, are rare and mostly concern internal organizational regulation; the exceptions named are the Security Council, which created the ICTY and ICTR, and European Union law.

terms.def: Conduct conforming to a recommendation is presumed lawful, even though the recommendation does not bind.

cards.q: A resolution is expressly non-binding. What legal effects can it still have?
cards.a: Members must consider it in good faith; conduct conforming to it enjoys a presumption of legality; it can catalyse custom by evidencing opinio iuris, or a treaty; and it supports argument before courts.

cards.q: Name the two standard examples of organs whose decisions are genuinely binding externally.
cards.a: The UN Security Council — which created the ICTY and ICTR by binding decision — and the institutions of the European Union.

slides.title: The Chagos Advisory Opinion
slides.text: The slide shows only a title, a photograph of a Chagossian protester holding a sign reading 'The UK took our island home for a US Air Base', and a map placing the Chagos Islands in the middle of the Indian Ocean. The advisory opinion of 2019 held that the decolonization of Mauritius had not been lawfully completed, because the Chagos Archipelago was detached before independence, and that the United Kingdom is under an obligation to end its administration as rapidly as possible. The slide itself gives none of that reasoning, so verify it against the lecture — it is placed here as an example of the General Assembly using its power to request advisory opinions.
slides.note: The slide contains no text beyond the title. The substance of the opinion is supplied from general knowledge — confirm against the lecture.

slides.title: The United Nations in outline
slides.text: Founded after the Second World War at San Francisco in 1945. Its main purpose is maintaining peace, pursued through two routes that map onto two chapters of the Charter: pacific settlement of disputes under Chapter VI and the system of collective security under Chapter VII. Seats in New York, Geneva, Vienna (from 1979) and Nairobi (from 1998); six official languages — Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian, Spanish; six principal organs — General Assembly, Security Council, ECOSOC, the defunct Trusteeship Council, the ICJ and the Secretariat; and seventeen specialized agencies.

cards.q: Name the six principal organs of the UN and say which is defunct.
cards.a: General Assembly, Security Council, Economic and Social Council, Trusteeship Council (defunct), International Court of Justice, Secretariat.

cards.q: Which two chapters of the UN Charter carry the Organization's main purpose, and what does each contain?
cards.a: Chapter VI, pacific settlement of disputes, and Chapter VII, the system of collective security including binding measures and the authorization of force.

slides.title: The General Assembly's competences
slides.text: All 193 members sit here, and the Charter gives it six kinds of power. It considers general principles of cooperation in maintaining peace and security, including disarmament, and recommends to members and the Council (Art 11(1)). It discusses specific disputes and may recommend — but under Article 12 only where the Security Council is NOT dealing with the matter (Art 11(2), 12). It initiates studies and recommendations across the political, economic, social, humanitarian, cultural, educational and health fields, and for the progressive development and codification of international law (Art 13). It receives reports from the Council and other organs (Art 15). It considers and approves the budget (Art 17). And it elects the non-permanent members of the Council and appoints the Secretary-General on the Council's recommendation.

cards.q: May the General Assembly make recommendations on a dispute the Security Council is currently seised of?
cards.a: No. Article 12 bars the Assembly from making recommendations on a dispute while the Security Council is exercising its functions in respect of it, unless the Council so requests.

cards.q: Which article of the Charter grounds the General Assembly's work on codification, and which body does that work?
cards.a: Article 13; the work is done by the International Law Commission, a subsidiary organ of the Assembly.

slides.title: The six main committees
slides.text: The Assembly works through six committees, and knowing which handles what is worth a mark: First — Disarmament and International Security; Second — Economic and Financial; Third — Social, Humanitarian and Cultural; Fourth — Special Political and Decolonization; Fifth — Administrative and Budgetary; Sixth — Legal. The Sixth Committee is where the ILC's work is debated.

cards.q: Which committee of the UN General Assembly handles legal questions, and which handles the budget?
cards.a: The Sixth Committee is the Legal Committee; the Fifth is Administrative and Budgetary.

slides.title: What the Security Council does
slides.text: It has PRIMARY — not exclusive — responsibility for maintaining international peace and security. Some of its decisions are binding, depending on intent. It recommends to the Assembly the appointment of the Secretary-General and the admission of new members, and together with the Assembly it elects the judges of the ICJ. Note the pattern: on the Organization's most important personnel and membership decisions, the two organs must act together.

slides.title: The Council's composition and voting
slides.text: Fifteen members: five permanent — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — and ten non-permanent elected for two years. A decision needs nine votes out of fifteen. On top of that sits the veto of the five permanent members, and the crucial qualification: the veto applies only to NON-PROCEDURAL matters. Whether a question is procedural is itself a substantive question, which is the famous double veto problem.

terms.def: A negative vote by a permanent member preventing adoption of a non-procedural decision of the Security Council.

cards.q: How many votes does a Security Council decision need, and when does the veto apply?
cards.a: Nine of fifteen. The veto of a permanent member applies only to non-procedural (substantive) matters; procedural decisions need only the nine votes.

slides.title: ECOSOC and the UN family
slides.text: The Economic and Social Council coordinates the economic and social work of the seventeen specialized agencies, five regional commissions and eleven UN funds and programmes. Beside them stand the 'related organizations' — the WTO, the IAEA, the CTBTO and the OPCW — which are linked to the UN but are not specialized agencies. The distinction matters because specialized agencies are brought into relationship with the UN by agreement under the Charter, while related organizations are not.

terms.def: An autonomous organization brought into relationship with the UN by agreement, its work coordinated by ECOSOC (e.g. ILO, WHO, UNESCO).

cards.q: Which UN organ coordinates the specialized agencies, and which bodies are 'related organizations' rather than agencies?
cards.a: ECOSOC coordinates the specialized agencies. The WTO, IAEA, CTBTO and OPCW are related organizations, linked to the UN without being specialized agencies.

slides.title: What ECOSOC is for
slides.text: Six functions in the diagram: promoting a higher standard of living, full employment and economic and social progress; solving international economic, social and health problems; international cooperation in culture and education; strengthening global respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms; and making recommendations and programmes for member states and the UN system. The last box gives the scale that surprises people — roughly 70 per cent of the personnel and financial resources of the UN sit in this broad mandate, not in the peace and security work.

cards.q: Roughly what share of UN personnel and financial resources belongs to the economic and social mandate?
cards.a: About 70 per cent — the broad ECOSOC mandate, not peace and security, accounts for most of the Organization's resources.

slides.title: Section: the International Court of Justice
slides.text: A section divider introducing the principal judicial organ.

slides.title: The composition of the ICJ
slides.text: Seated in The Hague, fifteen judges elected for nine years, five every three years, re-election permitted. They must be persons of high moral character who either qualify for the highest judicial office in their own countries or are recognized jurists in international law; as a body they must represent the main forms of civilization and the principal legal systems of the world. Nominations come not from governments but from the 'national groups' in the Permanent Court of Arbitration, and the General Assembly and the Security Council elect — both organs, separately and by absolute majority.

cards.q: Who nominates and who elects the judges of the ICJ?
cards.a: Nominations come from the national groups in the Permanent Court of Arbitration, not from governments directly; the General Assembly and the Security Council then both elect, each by its own majority.

slides.title: The Secretariat and the Secretary-General
slides.text: The Secretariat manages the Organization's administrative tasks. The Secretary-General is elected for five years by the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council, re-election permitted, and holds four roles at once: highest diplomat of the UN, chief administrative officer, provider of GOOD OFFICES for peaceful settlement, and mediator between parties to a dispute. The last two are political functions attached to an administrative office, which is the source of the post's influence.

terms.def: A third party's assistance in bringing disputing parties into contact, without proposing terms of settlement.

cards.q: How is the UN Secretary-General appointed, and what are the functions of the office?
cards.a: Elected for five years by the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council. Functions: highest diplomat, chief administrative officer, good offices for peaceful settlement, and mediation between parties to a dispute.

slides.title: Section: the UN Human Rights Council
slides.text: A section divider.

slides.title: The Human Rights Council
slides.text: Forty-seven members, created by a General Assembly resolution of 15 March 2006 to replace the fifty-three-member Commission on Human Rights, whose credibility had collapsed. It investigates situations of violations and adopts recommendations. Two mechanisms were built in to answer the old criticism: members must meet the 'highest standards' of human rights and undergo periodic review, and membership can be suspended by a two-thirds majority in the General Assembly.

terms.def: The mechanism by which every UN member's human rights record is reviewed in turn by the Human Rights Council.

cards.q: What was built into the Human Rights Council in 2006 that the old Commission lacked?
cards.a: A requirement that members meet the highest human rights standards and undergo periodic review, and the possibility of suspending a member's rights by a two-thirds majority of the General Assembly.

slides.title: Vienna as a conference city
slides.text: Two photographs with captions: the Kennedy-Khrushchev summit of 3–4 June 1961, and the conclusion of the Iran nuclear deal at the UNO City in July 2015. The point is the one Austria's neutrality was designed to produce — a venue acceptable to both sides.

slides.title: Vienna organizations I: UNHCR and IAEA
slides.text: UNHCR, the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, founded in 1951 and present in Vienna since 1951, though its headquarters is Geneva; its tasks are compliance with the international refugee agreements and material aid. The IAEA, the International Atomic Energy Agency, founded in 1957 and in Vienna from the start; its tasks are the peaceful use of nuclear energy and monitoring the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty since 1970.

cards.q: What does the IAEA do, and since when has it monitored the NPT?
cards.a: It promotes the peaceful use of nuclear energy and has monitored compliance with the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty since 1970. Founded 1957, seated in Vienna.

slides.title: Vienna organizations II: CTBTO and OSCE
slides.text: The CTBTO Preparatory Commission, in Vienna since 1997, works to obtain ratifications and signatures of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty of 1996 and operates a global monitoring system of seismic, hydroacoustic and infrasound measurements — note that it is still a PREPARATORY commission, because the treaty has not entered into force. The OSCE, in Vienna since 1995, succeeded the CSCE as a platform between East and West; the slide notes that its character as an international organization is DISPUTED, because it was never founded by a treaty.

cards.q: Why is the OSCE's status as an international organization disputed?
cards.a: Because it grew out of the CSCE process without a founding treaty. Under the ILC definition an IO must be established by a treaty or other instrument governed by international law and have its own legal personality.

cards.q: Why does the CTBTO still exist only as a Preparatory Commission?
cards.a: Because the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty of 1996 has not entered into force; the Commission works to obtain the necessary signatures and ratifications while already running the global monitoring system.

slides.title: Vienna organizations III: UNIDO and OPEC
slides.text: UNIDO, the UN Industrial Development Organization, founded 1966 and in Vienna from 1967, works on poverty reduction through productive capacity, trade capacity building, and energy and environment. OPEC, founded 1960 and in Vienna since 1965, is described on the slide with unusual frankness as an international oil cartel that sets production quotas — a reminder that an international organization need not pursue a public-interest purpose to be one.

slides.title: OPEC
slides.text: A picture slide on OPEC, without further text.

slides.title: The Vienna International Centre
slides.text: A photograph of the UN complex in Vienna, repeated from the previous lecture.

slides.title: What the organizations are worth to Austria
slides.text: The cover of a 2020 study by Jan Kluge and Alexander Schnabl, commissioned by the Austrian Ministry for European and International Affairs, on the economic effects of international organizations in Austria, beside a photograph of the IAEA Director General. It is on the slide as the practical answer to why a state competes to host organizations: the headquarters agreement costs privileges and immunities, and buys employment and international standing.
slides.note: The study cover is in German; the slide reproduces no figures from it.

slides.title: Section: the significance of IOs today
slides.text: A section divider with an illustration; the substantive discussion is oral.

slides.title: Review: define the terms
slides.text: The lecturer's own revision list, and the first item is pure definition work: international organizations; universal and regional organizations; supranational organizations; non-governmental organizations. If you can produce the ILC definition, the three classification axes and the founding-instrument test for NGOs, you have all four.

cards.q: Define universal, regional, supranational and non-governmental organizations in one line each.
cards.a: Universal: open to all states. Regional: membership limited to a region. Supranational: members transferred competences extensive enough for it to bind their citizens directly (EU). Non-governmental: an international organization NOT established by international agreement.

slides.title: Review: voting and decision-making
slides.text: Two revision questions: which exceptions exist to 'one state, one vote', and what forms of decision-making organizations use, with an example. Both were answered in the previous lecture — the veto, weighted voting and consensus on the first; unanimity and the varieties of majority on the second.

cards.q: Name the forms of decision-making in international organizations, with an example of each.
cards.a: Unanimity (EU common foreign and security policy); simple majority; qualified majority such as two thirds (UN GA important questions); weighted voting (IMF, World Bank); and consensus without a vote (OSCE, WTO).

slides.title: Review: legal status of organizations and staff
slides.text: The question asks for the legal status of organizations and their staff, the relevant legal sources, and the role of the host state's legal system. The answer has three layers: personality, derivative and functional, from the founding treaty; immunities from the founding treaty and the headquarters agreement, functional in rationale but absolute in practice for the organization and limited to official acts for staff; and the host state's law, which applies at the seat except where displaced, since inviolability is not extraterritoriality.

cards.q: Set out the legal status of an international organization and its staff, and the sources it comes from.
cards.a: Personality: derivative and functional, from the founding treaty (Bernadotte). Immunities: from the founding treaty and the headquarters agreement — absolute in practice for the organization, functional (official acts only) for staff, absolute for the highest officials. Host state law applies at the seat except as displaced; the premises are inviolable but not extraterritorial.

slides.title: Review: specialized agencies
slides.text: What are the UN's specialized agencies, three examples, and which organ is primarily responsible for them. The answer: autonomous organizations brought into relationship with the UN by agreement — for example the ILO, the WHO and UNESCO — coordinated by ECOSOC.

cards.q: What is a UN specialized agency, give three examples, and which organ is responsible for them?
cards.a: An autonomous international organization brought into relationship with the UN by agreement — e.g. the ILO, WHO and UNESCO — with coordination by the Economic and Social Council.

slides.title: Case: Avarika withdraws (a) and (b)
slides.text: The state of Avarika, under domestic pressure over its contributions to a UN specialized agency, decides to withdraw, leaving the agency in financial difficulty; the agency's General Assembly then decides to found its own research institute to earn money from research contracts. Two questions: may a state withdraw where the founding treaty does not provide for it, and may the organization establish a research institute where the founding treaty does not provide for that either? The two halves test the same idea from both sides — what may be done without an express provision.

cards.q: May a state withdraw from an organization whose founding treaty is silent on withdrawal?
cards.a: Yes on the prevailing view: sovereignty allows it, and Indonesia's 1965 withdrawal from the UN is the precedent. Some argue it depends on the nature of the organization and the parties' intention, so state the counter-argument too.

cards.q: May an organization set up a research institute where its founding treaty does not provide for it?
cards.a: Yes if the institute is necessary for the effective fulfilment of its tasks — the implied powers doctrine (Bernadotte, Certain Expenses). If it serves a purpose outside the organization's competences, the act is ultra vires.

slides.title: Case: Avarika continued (c), (d), (e)
slides.text: The institute rents a building in the host state Domizilia and hires Mr Explorator as managing director; when it proves unprofitable the organization halves his salary, and he sues in the Domizilian labour court, seeking enforcement against the organization's assets. Three questions: may the organization rent premises and conclude an employment contract; will his action succeed; and can the judgment be enforced against the organization's assets?

cards.q: May an international organization rent office space and employ staff in its host state? On what basis?
cards.a: Yes — on the basis of its legal personality under the DOMESTIC law of the host state, which is distinct from its international legal personality and gives it capacity to acquire property, contract and employ.

cards.q: An employee sues an international organization in the host state's labour court. Prospects?
cards.a: Poor. The organization enjoys immunity from domestic jurisdiction — in practice absolute, with no imperii/gestionis distinction — so the court must decline. His route is the organization's administrative tribunal; that alternative remedy is what keeps the immunity from being a denial of justice.

cards.q: Can a judgment be enforced against an international organization's assets in the host state?
cards.a: No. Immunity from enforcement is separate and, for organizations, effectively absolute; the assets and archives are inviolable under the headquarters agreement, so execution requires the organization's consent.

slides.title: Case: the furniture from Döbling (a)
slides.text: Mr Großmann, a department manager at the IOSD in Vienna, orders office furniture for €100,000 from Organic Wood GmbH and a kitchen for his weekend house for €50,000, paying a €5,000 deposit out of a donation made to the organization. The organization refuses the invoice for want of internal authorization, dismisses him and reports him to the police. The first question is whether the carpenter can sue the organization in Vienna for the office furniture. Two issues hide in it: whether the organization is bound by an act exceeding internal authorization, and whether a Viennese court may hear the claim at all.

cards.q: A supplier sues an international organization in Vienna for goods ordered by an official without internal authorization. Can the court hear the case?
cards.a: No — the organization's immunity from Austrian jurisdiction bars it, and unlike state immunity it is not lost for commercial acts. Whether the organization is internally bound by an unauthorized order is a separate question the court never reaches.

slides.title: Case: the furniture, continued (b)-(f)
slides.text: Five follow-ups: would it differ if the order had come from a foreign embassy; how else can the supplier assert its rights and where is that regulated; can it sue for the private kitchen; where can Großmann challenge his dismissal; and can the Austrian criminal proceedings against him go ahead. Each turns on a distinction the lecture has already drawn — organization immunity versus state immunity, official versus private acts, and functional immunity of staff.

cards.q: Would the supplier's claim differ if the order had come from a foreign EMBASSY rather than an international organization?
cards.a: Yes. A state enjoys only restrictive immunity: furnishing an embassy is arguably an acta iure gestionis commercial transaction, so the Austrian court could have jurisdiction (Art 10 UN Convention; Dralle). An organization's immunity by contrast covers commercial acts too.

cards.q: Can the supplier sue for the kitchen ordered for the official's private weekend house?
cards.a: Yes — against the official personally. That order was a private act, not an official one, so the staff member's functional immunity does not cover it and the organization was never a party.

cards.q: Where does a dismissed official of an international organization challenge the dismissal?
cards.a: Before the organization's administrative tribunal — UNAT, ILOAT or the equivalent — because the organization's immunity excludes the domestic labour courts.

cards.q: Can Austria prosecute an official for misappropriating the organization's funds?
cards.a: It depends whether the act was official. Functional immunity covers official acts only; misusing a donation for a private purchase is not an official act, so prosecution is possible — and in any event the organization can waive immunity, which is what filing the complaint implies.

slides.title: Review: establishment, members, specialized agencies
slides.text: How are organizations usually established and who are their members; what are the specialized agencies, in which fields do they work, two examples. Established by a founding treaty governed by international law; members are states and sometimes other organizations; the agencies work in labour, health, education, aviation, food and so on — the ILO and the WHO will do as examples.

slides.title: Review: consultative status
slides.text: What consultative status at the UN means, which organizations can obtain it, and what rights it carries. The basis is Article 71 of the Charter: ECOSOC may make arrangements for consultation with non-governmental organizations. The status gives NGOs access — the right to attend meetings, to submit written statements and, in some categories, to speak — but no vote and no legal personality. It is the formal answer to why NGOs matter in practice while remaining outside the circle of subjects.

terms.def: Arrangements under Art 71 UN Charter allowing an NGO to attend ECOSOC meetings and submit statements; it confers access, not membership or personality.

cards.q: What does consultative status at the UN give an NGO, and what does it not give?
cards.a: Access under Article 71 UN Charter — attendance at ECOSOC meetings, written statements and, in some categories, oral interventions. It gives no vote, no membership and no international legal personality.

slides.title: Review: determining legal personality
slides.text: How the legal personality of an organization is determined, with an example from practice. Two routes: express conferral in the founding treaty, and — where the treaty is silent — inference from the organization's functions and powers, which is exactly what the ICJ did in Bernadotte for the UN. Give the case; it is the answer the question is fishing for.

cards.q: How is the international legal personality of an organization determined where its founding treaty does not say?
cards.a: By inference from its functions, organs and powers — the objective approach taken by the ICJ in the Bernadotte opinion, where the UN's personality followed from what the Charter required it to do.

slides.title: Case: cocaine at the airport
slides.text: A UN staff member travelling from Vienna to the General Assembly is found with five grams of cocaine at the airport and is prosecuted in Austria. The judge says the UN has no international legal personality under its statutes so its employees have no special status; the intern says the employee was on official duty so nothing can be done, and adds that organizations have their own tribunals to try their staff. When he ignores the summons, Austrian officers enter the Vienna International Centre to arrest him. Every proposition in that paragraph is wrong in a different way — which is why it is such a good exam question.

cards.q: A judge says the UN 'has no international legal personality under its statutes', so its staff enjoy no special status. Correct?
cards.a: No. The UN's personality does not depend on being written into the Charter: the ICJ inferred it from the Organization's functions in Bernadotte, and staff privileges rest on the Convention on Privileges and Immunities and the headquarters agreement in any event.

cards.q: Does a UN official's immunity cover carrying cocaine while travelling to a General Assembly session?
cards.a: No. Staff immunity is functional — official acts only. Travelling on duty does not make possession of drugs an official act, so Austria may prosecute. Only the highest-ranking officials enjoy immunity beyond official acts.

cards.q: May Austrian police enter the Vienna International Centre to arrest a staff member who ignored a summons?
cards.a: Not without the UN's consent. The seat is inviolable under Article III of the headquarters agreement and is under UN control and authority; Austrian law applies inside, but the authorities may not enter to enforce it.

cards.q: Do international organizations have tribunals that can try their staff for crimes?
cards.a: No. UNAT and ILOAT are employment tribunals deciding disputes between the organization and its staff; they have no criminal jurisdiction. Criminal matters remain with national courts, subject to functional immunity and waiver.
